reference_answer_draft: The simulator is CaloGAN, a generative adversarial network (GAN); it is not CaloFlow and this paper does not introduce it as WGAN.
A shower is represented by three 2D images of per-cell deposited energy, with layer dimensions 3×96, 12×12 and 12×6.
The generator uses a convolutional U-net encoder-decoder with skip connections linking encoding and decoding layers at the same spatial resolution.

The study reports speed-ups up to about three orders of magnitude, depending on hardware; WGAN evaluation time is independent of incident electron energy, unlike GEANT4. This is a setup-specific benchmark, not a universal performance guarantee.

Flow I models layer-wise deposited energies conditioned on incident energy. Flow II models voxel-level shower shapes conditioned on those layer energies and incident energy. The two-step design improves the treatment of energy conservation compared with the tested single-flow alternatives.

CaloGAN uses adversarial GAN training and an implicit density without an explicit likelihood. CaloFlow uses normalizing flows with explicit tractable likelihoods and likelihood-based training/model selection. CaloGAN is not itself a normalizing flow.

The jet study maps particle-level hadronic-jet images to reconstructed jet images, using CMS samples represented by 32×32 pixels. The WGAN study generates isolated electromagnetic-shower energy depositions in a seven-sensitive-layer sampling calorimeter prototype. Jet images and multilayer electromagnetic showers must not be conflated.

Both describe penalizing the absolute difference between requested/nominal and reconstructed energy. The companion specifies a mean absolute error term augmenting the adversarial loss and states that the soft constraint discourages but does not forbid excess deposited energy; it is not an exact hard guarantee.
